name: Anuradhapura
info: Anuradhapura is a city in the north central plain of Sri Lanka, on the Malwathu Oya, settled from about the 10th century BCE, the long-serving ancient capital of the Sinhalese and a centre of Theravada Buddhism.

facts.founded: The Mahāvaṃsa places the founding of the city in 437 BCE and tells that a minister named Anuradha founded a village near the Kadamba river, which King Pandukabhaya later made the capital; excavations date human settlement on the site to the 10th century BCE.
facts.where: On the banks of the Malwathu Oya in the north central plain of Sri Lanka, 205 km north of Colombo, in the North Central Province.
facts.known: The ancient capital of the Sinhalese kingdom for about 1,500 years; a centre of Theravada Buddhism; the Maha Viharaya and the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi; the stupas and monasteries of its sacred city; the Chola invasion of 993 and its abandonment
facts.today: Anuradhapura is the capital of the North Central Province and of Anuradhapura District, with a World Heritage Site of ancient ruins beside a planned New Town.

t: Excavations show settlement on the site from the 10th century BCE, while the Mahāvaṃsa places the founding of the city in 437 BCE and tells that Pandukabhaya made it the capital of the Sinhalese kingdom.
Anuradhapura was the Sinhalese capital for about 1,500 years and a centre of Theravada Buddhism, with a network of temples and monasteries that now covers over 100 square kilometres.
After the Chola invasions of 993 and 1014 the city was largely deserted and the capital moved to Polonnaruwa, but it stayed a pilgrimage site and was revived under British rule from the 1870s.
dyk: The Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, a tree at Anuradhapura, is held to be the oldest still-living, documented, planted tree in the world and is believed to have originated from the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, under which the Buddha attained enlightenment.

sections.origins:
Anuradhapura lies on the banks of the Malwathu Oya, known in the Mahāvaṃsa as the Kadamba river, in the north central plain of Sri Lanka. The land around it was irrigable and fertile, major ports lay to the north-west and north-east of the island, and the dense jungle around the city gave it a natural defence.

According to the Mahāvaṃsa, Vijaya's ministers founded villages here and there, and a minister named Anuradha built Anuradhagama near the Kadamba river; gama means village. The chronicle places the founding of the city in 437 BCE and tells that King Pandukabhaya, whose reign is given as 474 to 367 BCE, laid out the city of Anuradhapura and established it as the capital in 377 BCE. As the settlement became an urban centre its name changed to Anuradhapura, pura meaning city. Archaeological evidence from the citadel area puts human settlement on the site as far back as the 10th century BCE. The protohistoric Iron Age of the city spans 900 to 600 BCE, with iron technology, pottery, the horse, domestic cattle and paddy cultivation, and between 700 and 600 BCE the settlement grew over an area of at least 50 hectares. Plain Grey Ware of 600 to 500 BCE shows connections with North India.
sections.growth:
The Sinhalese chronicles are the source for the city's development between 500 and 250 BCE. According to these records, Pandukabhaya planned the city formally, with gates and quarters for traders. It then covered an area of one square kilometre, which made it one of the largest cities in Asia at the time.

Anuradhapura became the centre of Theravada Buddhism for many centuries and a major pilgrimage site. It was home to Buddhist philosophers, among them Buddhaghosa. During the reign of Dhatusena, 455 to 473, a redaction of the Theravada canon took place, 18 new vihara were built and a statue was erected for Mahinda, the Indian prince-monk who introduced Buddhism to the island. In the late Anuradhapura period the royal family and the nobility supported Buddhism strongly and commissioned works of art, which they donated to temples; in return the temples and the local Buddhist community supported the king's rule. Depictions of Avalokitesvara, the Bodhisattva of Mercy and Compassion, became increasingly popular. The temples and monasteries now cover over 100 square kilometres.
sections.rulers:
Anuradhapura was the first capital of the Sinhala Kingdom of Rajarata, which followed the kingdoms of Tambapanni and Upatissa Nuwara. Its history as a royal city runs from the reign of Pandukabhaya to the abandonment of the city by the last of the Anuradhapura kings at the end of the 10th century CE. It served from 437 BCE to 1017 CE, about 1,500 years, which made it the longest-serving ancient capital of the Sinhalese.

The Chola king Rajaraja I invaded in 993, and his son Rajendra I followed in 1014. After the first invasion the political centre shifted to Polonnaruwa. Later Sinhalese kings tried to return the capital to Anuradhapura, and the city was briefly reoccupied in the 11th century. Some of its major monuments were restored in the late 13th century by Vijayabahu IV, who reigned from 1267 to 1270. Under British colonial rule Anuradhapura became an administrative centre, and by the early 20th century it was designated the administrative centre of the North Central Province.
sections.life:
Anuradhapura was an intellectual centre of early Theravada Buddhism, and its monasteries stood at the centre of its religious life. The Maha Viharaya and the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi were its best-known places of worship, and the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi was believed to have grown from the original Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. Other places of veneration included the Ruwanwelisaya, the Thuparamaya, the Lovamahapaya, the Abhayagiri Dagaba, the Jetavanarama, the Mirisaveti Stupa and the Lankarama.

When the city was planned under Pandukabhaya it was given gates and quarters for traders. Excavation shows connections with North India as early as 600 to 500 BCE, and Claudius Ptolemy, writing in the 2nd century CE, named a place called Anourogrammoi among the cities of Taprobane, which scholars widely read as Anuradhagama or Anuradhapura. Among the other structures of the ancient city are the Isurumuniya, the Kuttam Pokuna, the Ranmasu Uyana and the Rathna Prasadaya.
sections.crises:
The city was mostly destroyed and largely deserted after the Chola invasion of 993, which Rajaraja I led, and his son Rajendra I invaded again in 1014. According to the Culavamsa, Anuradhapura was utterly destroyed in every way by the Chola army. The place was nevertheless continuously inhabited afterwards, as the records of visitors such as Robert Knox show. The Cholas' invasions ended its time as the main population centre of the island, and it was not re-established as one until the British colonial era in the 19th century.

The area was sparsely inhabited for many centuries. Robert Knox wrote in 1681 that a watch was kept at the city, beyond which were no more people who obeyed the King of Kandy. In 1821 John Davy described Anuradhapura, so long the capital of Ceylon, as a small mean village in the midst of a desert, with a large tank, numerous stone pillars and two or three immense mounds, probably old dagobas, as its principal remains; he added that it was still considered a sacred spot and a place of pilgrimage.
sections.legacy:
Anuradhapura remained a vital pilgrimage site for Buddhists throughout the medieval period and continues to be one. Its revival began in the 1870s under British colonial rule, with infrastructure and urban planning meant to support administration and to receive pilgrims, and in the late 19th century the British authorities began archaeological surveys and restoration. The opening of the Northern Railway line and the railway station in 1904 made the town a transport hub.

In 1949 the Government of Ceylon began the Anuradhapura Preservation Plan, drawn up by Oliver Weerasinghe, to protect the ancient city by building a separate planned township, the New Town, to the east. Government offices and law courts were moved there and the Anuradhapura Preservation Board was set up. From 1958 to 1962 Nissanka Wijeyeratne served as Government Agent and chairman of the board during the move of the old city's residents. Anuradhapura was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. It is the capital of the North Central Province and of Anuradhapura District, and the headquarters of Sri Lanka's archaeological survey.

summary: Anuradhapura, on the Malwathu Oya in northern Sri Lanka, was settled from about the 10th century BCE and was the Sinhalese capital for about 1,500 years and a centre of Theravada Buddhism. It was largely deserted after the Chola invasion of 993 and was revived under British rule.
notes: SOURCE: only the city's own article exists (no history article); it is short, so several sections run under 1,100 characters rather than being padded.

START: the Mahavamsa gives 437 BCE for the founding; excavations give human settlement from the 10th century BCE, and the Iron Age phase 900 to 600 BCE. I used -900, circa true, and give both in facts.

INTERNAL CONFLICT: the article says Pandukabhaya (474-367 BCE) laid out the city and made it capital in 377 BCE, and also says it was 'laid out by Devanampiya Tissa (250-210 BCE)'. I left Devanampiya Tissa out. It also says the Mahavamsa dates from the 5th century CE and, in the same breath, places the founding in the 5th century BC.

CHOLA DATES: the article gives 993 (Rajaraja I) and 1014 (Rajendra I) for the invasions, 'the end of the tenth century' for abandonment, a 'brief reoccupation in the eleventh', and 'until the 11th century CE (1017 CE)' for the capital's span. I kept all as given; 'about 1,500 years' is the article's own figure (437 BCE to 1017 CE is about 1,450). The Culavamsa is dated '6th century CE-18th century CE' in the article, which I did not repeat.
The article says the political centre shifted to Polonnaruwa after the Chola conquest; no dates given for that move.
Dhatusena: 455-473 as given; the article does not say the canon redaction or the vihara were at Anuradhapura beyond the context of the section. Event label '455' is the reign's start.

Left out as not history or not in the article's own terms: tourism, the airport, climate, transport routes, demographics (the article has a census heading with no figures), the Vessagiriya and other structures listed without description, and the Wijeyeratne memorial to H. R. Freeman.
Ptolemy's Anourogrammoi: the article says 'scholars widely interpret' it as Anuradhagama/Anuradhapura; hedged accordingly.

Modern article claims about the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi ('oldest still-living, documented, planted tree') are given as the article's description; the article says 'believed to have originated' from the Bodh Gaya tree.
Present size: the article gives no population figure.
